strengths: Addresses an important and hitherto underrepresented domain in LLM evaluation, bridging the gap between high-level software benchmarks and hardware RTL synthesis by evaluating conceptual and analytical reasoning in computer architecture.

Rigorous data curation process incorporating multiple pipelines (synthetic generation, academic exams, and an expert crowdsourcing platform) along with human expert validation by domain specialists across all 2,671 question-answer pairs.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 10 frontier models in the main paper and 26 models overall, spanning diverse model scales, reasoning variants, and modalities (including 548 multimodal questions).

Thorough validation of the LLM-as-a-Judge methodology on free-response questions, comparing 908 model generations against a cohort of 11 domain experts and achieving an 85.35% human-LLM agreement rate (closely approaching the 90.7% inter-human agreement rate).

Detailed qualitative analysis identifying specific, concrete architectural reasoning failure modes (e.g., microarchitectural semantics of code, system state tracking, implicit default conventions, and multimodal spatial interpretation).
weaknesses: Substantial class imbalance across the four cognitive skills: while Recall (1,564) and Analyze (995) have broad coverage, Design (35) and Implement (77) have relatively few questions, which limits statistical significance and increases variance when tracking fine-grained design progress.

The majority of questions (1,547 out of 2,671, or ~58%) are synthetically generated cloze-style multiple-choice questions focusing heavily on factual recall rather than complex multi-step architectural reasoning.

Potential risk of pretraining data contamination, particularly for questions scraped from publicly accessible university course websites and open-access publications, which are commonly indexed in frontier LLM web corpora.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored niche in LLM evaluation: existing computing systems benchmarks focus largely on RTL/code generation or software engineering, whereas QUARCH evaluates conceptual, analytical, and design trade-off reasoning in computer architecture.

Comprehensive benchmark scale and curation effort: curating 2,671 expert-validated question-answer pairs with contributions from over 140 experts across 40 institutions, integrating academic exams, crowdsourcing, and synthetic generation.

Rigorous validation of the evaluation methodology: the authors conduct a robust study comparing LLM-as-a-judge against domain expert consensus across 908 model responses, demonstrating an 85.35% agreement rate that approaches inter-human agreement (90.7%).

Nuanced evaluation across 26 models and thorough qualitative failure analyses, identifying concrete domain-specific weaknesses such as modeling hardware-software execution semantics, tracking system state (e.g., cache coherence protocols), and multimodal schematic interpretation.
Clear structure and categorization framework dividing tasks into Recall, Analyze, Design, and Implement, allowing fine-grained tracking of model capability beyond monolithic benchmark scores.
weaknesses: Skewed skill distribution: higher-order tasks such as Design (35 QAs) and Implement (77 QAs) constitute less than 4.2% of the entire benchmark combined. While the authors explain the difficulty of sourcing these questions, sample sizes as small as 35 make fine-grained conclusions on design capabilities statistically less robust.

High proportion of synthetic recall items: over 57% (1,547 QAs) of the benchmark consists of synthetically generated cloze MCQs, which primarily measure surface-level factual memorization rather than multi-step architectural reasoning.

Contamination and benchmark longevity safeguards are minimally discussed: since many questions are drawn from university exams and public technical resources, future frontier models may easily suffer from data contamination without strict canary strings or private holdout splits.

strengths: Addresses an important and hitherto unaddressed gap in the LLM evaluation literature by focusing on conceptual and multi-objective reasoning in computer architecture, distinguishing itself from existing code generation (SWE-bench) and RTL generation (VerilogEval) benchmarks.

Well-structured conceptual framing grounded in four architectural competencies (Recall, Analyze, Design, Implement), providing clear diagnostic distinction between simple factual retrieval and higher-order analytical reasoning.

Comprehensive benchmark construction (2,671 expert-validated QA pairs across 13 core topics) combining university exams, expert crowdsourcing, and synthetically generated items with multi-stage human validation.

Rigorous evaluation methodology: Includes extensive evaluation of 26 models, robust pass@k=1 stochastic averaging (n=3), and a thorough validation of LLM-as-a-judge against 11 domain experts across 908 responses (achieving 85.35% agreement vs. 90.7% human-human agreement).

Detailed qualitative analysis and failure categorization in Section 4.3 and Appendix C, offering concrete insights into why frontier models fail (e.g., SIMD warp divergence, cache coherence state modeling, and hardware-software semantics in code execution).
weaknesses: Significant skill imbalance across the benchmark: Recall (1,564) and Analyze (995) make up over 95% of the dataset, whereas Design (35) and Implement (77) represent only ~4.2% combined, which limits statistical significance for conclusions drawn specifically on design and implementation skills.

Potential data contamination risk: A substantial portion of the dataset is scraped from publicly available university course exams, which may overlap with the pre-training corpora of web-scraped frontier LLMs; the manuscript lacks a formal decontamination or n-gram overlap analysis.

Heavy reliance on synthetic cloze-style multiple-choice questions for the Recall portion (1,547 of 2,671 items), which may inflate model recall scores and skew the overall distribution towards textbook definition retrieval rather than applied domain knowledge.

strengths: Addresses an important and neglected domain in foundation model evaluation by focusing on conceptual and analytical computer architecture reasoning rather than low-level code/RTL syntax generation.

Comprehensive benchmark curation combining synthetic generation, crowdsourcing, and academic exams, backed by thorough expert verification across 2,671 items with multimodal components (circuit schematics, pipeline diagrams, roofline plots).

Rigorous validation of the evaluation protocol: evaluates LLM-as-a-judge fidelity against 908 domain-expert human judgments across 11 experts, demonstrating strong agreement (85.48% vs. 90.75% human-human agreement) along with thorough analyses of judge bias and consistency.

In-depth analysis of failure modes (such as architecture-semantics of code execution, state tracking in coherence protocols, and default architectural assumptions) provides valuable, actionable insights for the community.

Demonstrates practical utility and knowledge transfer via realistic downstream hardware design case studies (memory hierarchy optimization and DRAM controller tuning), showing measurable improvements after fine-tuning.
weaknesses: Significant distribution skew across skills: higher-order 'Design' (42 QAs) and 'Implement' (98 QAs) categories constitute only ~5% of the total dataset compared to 'Recall' (1,579) and 'Analyze' (952), which may reduce statistical robustness when evaluating those specific competencies.

The downstream transfer fine-tuning experiment relies on a narrow, highly task-specific subset of 45 memory questions; as noted by the authors, fine-tuning on diverse architecture topics did not yield similar gains, suggesting broader domain-wide transfer remains challenging.
While LLM-as-a-judge is well-validated, the ~14.5% disagreement rate with human experts on free-response questions could introduce noise when distinguishing between closely performing models.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored gap: while hardware code generation (RTL) and EDA script generation benchmarks exist, QUARCH is the first benchmark focused specifically on conceptual and analytical reasoning across the full computer architecture design space.

Well-structured conceptual skills framework (Recall, Analyze, Design, Implement) that effectively disentangles factual retrieval from multi-step architectural reasoning, revealing a substantial performance gap in current frontier models.
Rigorous data curation and validation pipeline combining synthetic generation, crowdsourced competitions, and academic exams, all vetted by domain experts.

Thorough and credible validation of LLM-as-a-Judge against domain human experts (11 experts grading 908 model responses across 100 questions), demonstrating an 85.48% human-LLM agreement rate that approaches human-to-human agreement (90.75%), complete with self-preference bias analyses.

Convincing downstream validation showing that fine-tuning on architectural reasoning QAs transfers positively to concrete architectural design space exploration tasks (e.g., Accelergy/Timeloop memory hierarchy design and DRAMSys controller tuning).
weaknesses: Skill distribution is heavily skewed toward Recall (1,579) and Analyze (952), with Design (42) and Implement (98) comprising only ~5% of the dataset. While the authors note the high difficulty of authoring these questions, the smaller sample size limits statistical power when drawing fine-grained conclusions on Design and Implement capabilities.

Academic exams scraped from university websites carry an inherent risk of pretraining data contamination for large web-scraped LLMs, though the private holdout set and synthetic/crowdsourced splits help partially mitigate this.

The fine-tuning case study relies on a relatively narrow subset (45 questions and matrix multiplication workloads); exploring whether fine-tuning on QUARCH generalizes across a wider variety of system architectures and workloads would strengthen the claims of generalizable knowledge transfer.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored gap in AI evaluation by targeting conceptual and analytical reasoning in computer architecture, bridging the divide between software engineering benchmarks (e.g., SWE-bench) and RTL/code generation benchmarks (e.g., VerilogEval).

Comprehensive benchmark construction featuring 2,671 expert-validated questions spanning 13 subfields, four cognitive skills (Recall, Analyze, Design, Implement), and multiple modalities (text and diagrams/schematics).

Extensive and rigorous model evaluation across 10 frontier models in the main paper and an additional 20 models in the appendix, providing clear evidence that while factual recall is largely mastered, models struggle significantly with higher-order architectural reasoning.

Thorough validation of the LLM-as-a-judge pipeline against domain experts (11 hardware architects grading 908 responses across 100 questions), demonstrating an 85.5% human-LLM agreement rate alongside thoughtful checks for self-preference bias and cross-judge consistency.

Convincing downstream validation showing knowledge transfer to realistic hardware design tasks (e.g., memory hierarchy exploration using Accelergy and DRAM controller tuning with DRAMSys), demonstrating tangible area and energy improvements after fine-tuning.
weaknesses: Severe class imbalance across the four cognitive competencies: Design (42 QAs) and Implement (98 QAs) together constitute barely 5% of the benchmark, which limits the statistical confidence of claims specifically targeting design and implementation capabilities.

The fine-tuning case study relies on a tightly filtered subset of only 45 questions specific to memory subsystems and GEMM rather than the broader benchmark, representing narrow domain-adaptation rather than broad generalization of architectural reasoning.
The static QA paradigm abstracts away interactive toolchain usage, iterative debugging, and closed-loop simulator feedback, which are fundamental components of real-world architectural workflows.

Evaluation on multimodal items reveals performance drops across all models, but the diagnostic analysis does not fully isolate whether failures stem from basic vision perception errors (e.g., OCR on datapath labels) versus high-level spatial/architectural reasoning.
